notice: Newly authored study material. Examples are fictional or generic, not classroom quotations or personal stories.

notes.title: Worth doing
notes.prompt:
worth to visit
or worth visiting?
notes.explanation: Use be worth + -ing to say that an activity deserves your time or effort.
notes.qualification: Time well spent and well worth visiting are also valid expressions.
notes.practice: Complete: It is worth ___ a little every day. (practise)
notes.answer: practising: It is worth practising a little every day.

notes.title: Spend time doing
notes.explanation: Use spend + time + -ing for an activity. Use spend + time or money + on + a noun phrase.
notes.qualification: Spent is the past form of spend.
examples: I spent some money on books.
notes.practice: Complete: I spend ten minutes ___ my notes. (review)
notes.answer: reviewing: I spend ten minutes reviewing my notes.

notes.title: One of my favourites
notes.prompt:
one of my favourite
sport or sports?
notes.explanation: One of selects one member from a group, so the noun naming that group is plural.
notes.qualification: When the whole subject is One of my friends, the main verb is normally singular.
examples: Swimming is one of my favourite sports.
One of my friends lives nearby.
notes.practice: Complete: One of my favourite ___ is reading. (activity)
notes.answer: activities: One of my favourite activities is reading.

notes.title: Is the past perfect required?
notes.prompt:
I did not call
before I went.
notes.explanation: This sentence can be correct. Before already makes the order clear. Past perfect can add an earlier viewpoint.
notes.qualification: Two past events do not automatically require the past perfect.
examples: I did not call before I went.
When I arrived, I realised I had not called.
notes.practice: Which event happened first? When I arrived, the class had started.
notes.answer: The class started before I arrived.

notes.title: Past or present perfect?
notes.explanation: Use past simple for an event at a finished past time. Present perfect connects experience or a result to now.
notes.qualification: No stated date does not automatically mean present perfect.
examples: I have visited that museum before.
notes.practice: Complete: I ___ that book last month. (read)
notes.answer: read, in the past simple. Its past pronunciation is /red/.

notes.title: For or since?
notes.explanation: For introduces a duration. Since introduces a starting point. Choose the tense according to the time relationship.
notes.qualification: For can also appear with past simple when the period has ended.
examples: I have lived here for two years.
I lived there for two years, then moved.
notes.practice: Complete: We have known each other ___ we were children.
notes.answer: since: the clause identifies the starting point.

notes.title: Have lived or been living?
notes.explanation: Use have lived or have been living for residence continuing to now. Have been lived does not express this meaning.
notes.qualification: The continuous form often emphasises the ongoing situation.
examples: I have lived here for a year.
I have been living here for a year.
notes.practice: Repair: I have been studied English recently.
notes.answer: I have been studying English recently.

notes.title: The background and the event
notes.prompt:
I was reading
when the phone rang.
notes.explanation: Past continuous presents an activity in progress. Past simple can introduce an event during that activity.
notes.qualification: The grammar does not prove that the background activity stopped.
examples: I was cooking when a friend called.
I cooked, ate, and washed the dishes.
notes.practice: Complete: We ___ when the teacher arrived. (talk)
notes.answer: were talking, if the talking was already in progress.

notes.title: Future plans have options
notes.prompt:
I am meeting
a friend tomorrow.
notes.explanation: Present continuous can describe an arrangement. Going to often describes an intention. Will can express predictions, offers, or decisions.
notes.qualification: These forms overlap; a planned event is not automatically wrong with will.
examples: I am meeting a friend tomorrow.
I will send you the details.
notes.practice: Write a sentence about a settled arrangement.
notes.answer: One possible answer: I am having lunch with a friend tomorrow.

notes.title: Used to or still?
notes.prompt:
We used to meet.
We still meet.
notes.explanation: Used to describes a past habit or state, normally suggesting it has changed. Still shows that something continues.
notes.qualification: Do not choose used to only because the topic mentions the past.
examples: We used to walk to school.
A past routine that has changed
We still walk together at weekends.
notes.practice: Which fits a habit that continues now: used to or still?
notes.answer: still: We still meet regularly.

notes.title: After did, use the base form
notes.prompt:
Did you went?
Did you go?
notes.explanation: In ordinary questions and negatives with did or did not, the main verb stays in its base form.
notes.qualification: The past tense is already carried by did.
examples: I did not buy it online.
notes.practice: Repair: I did not saw the message.
notes.answer: I did not see the message.

notes.title: Swam or swum?
notes.explanation: Perfect forms use a past participle after have, has, or had. Some participles differ from the simple past.
notes.qualification: Learn irregular verbs as three-part groups.
examples: I have never swum in a river.
notes.practice: Complete: She has ___ the answer. (write)
notes.answer: written. The three forms are write, wrote, written.

notes.title: A or an? Listen first.
notes.explanation: Choose a or an by the next sound, not simply the next letter. An goes before a vowel sound.
notes.qualification: A silent first letter can change the article you need.
examples: honest begins with a vowel sound.
notes.practice: Complete: It was ___ amazing experience.
notes.answer: an: amazing begins with a vowel sound.

notes.title: Some good news
notes.explanation: News, advice, and information are normally uncountable in these meanings. Use some or a countable unit such as a piece of.
notes.qualification: News ends in s but normally takes a singular verb.
examples: She gave me a piece of advice.
notes.practice: Repair: I received an information.
notes.answer: I received some information / a piece of information.

notes.title: Other or another?
notes.explanation: Other works with plural and uncountable nouns. Another usually introduces one additional singular countable item.
notes.qualification: The other person and another two days are also valid patterns.
notes.practice: Complete: Could you give me another ___ of advice?
notes.answer: piece: another piece of advice.

notes.title: A number of or the number of?
notes.explanation: A number of + plural noun normally takes a plural verb. The number of focuses on one total and takes a singular verb.
notes.qualification: Check the whole subject, not only the nearest noun.
examples: A number of students are waiting.
The number of students is increasing.
notes.practice: Complete: The number of visitors ___ growing.
notes.answer: is: the subject is the singular number.

notes.title: Let, make, and help
notes.explanation: Use let + person + base verb and active make + person + base verb. Help allows a base verb with or without to.
notes.qualification: Make + object + adjective is a different pattern: make the task easier.
examples: No to after let in this pattern.
helps me to speak is also valid.
notes.practice: Repair: It does not let me concentrated.
notes.answer: It does not let me concentrate.

notes.title: Easy for me
notes.prompt:
I am easy
to get there?
notes.explanation: Use It is easy for me to get there when the action is easy for you. You can also say I can get there easily.
notes.qualification: I am easy to contact is valid: other people can contact me easily.
examples: It is easy for me to get there.
The park is easy to reach.
The park can be reached easily.
notes.practice: Repair the intended meaning: I am easy to make mistakes.
notes.answer: I tend to make mistakes / It is easy for me to make mistakes.

notes.title: It happened
notes.explanation: Happen and occur are intransitive in this meaning. Use happened or occurred, without a passive was.
notes.qualification: Passive voice is valid with suitable verbs: The photo was taken yesterday.
notes.practice: Repair: The situation was occurred suddenly.
notes.answer: The situation occurred suddenly / It happened suddenly.

notes.title: Consists of
notes.prompt:
consists of
or is composed of
notes.explanation: Use consists of to say what something contains. Alternatively, use is composed of or is made up of.
notes.qualification: Do not combine is with the base form consist.
examples: The course consists of three parts.
The course is made up of three parts.
notes.practice: Repair: The system is consist of several parts.
notes.answer: The system consists of several parts.

notes.title: Questions with be and do
notes.prompt:
Is she friendly?
Does she like art?
notes.explanation: With be, put be before the subject. With an ordinary present-simple verb, use do or does and the base verb.
notes.qualification: What is she like? asks about character. What does she like? asks about preferences.
notes.practice: Repair: Does she is interested in art?
notes.answer: Is she interested in art?

notes.title: Keep a list parallel
notes.explanation: When several activities share enjoy as their verb, use -ing for each activity.
notes.qualification: Separate clauses can use different forms: I enjoy reading, and I walk every day.
examples: I enjoy reading and taking notes.
I enjoy reading, and I take notes.
notes.practice: Complete: I enjoy swimming and ___ time outdoors. (spend)
notes.answer: spending, when both activities depend on enjoy.

notes.title: Hope or wish?
notes.prompt:
I wish you
have a good time?
notes.explanation: For an ordinary positive hope about a future experience, use hope + clause. Wish can take a person and a noun phrase.
notes.qualification: These are different patterns, not simply different levels of politeness.
examples: I hope you have a good time.
I wish you a pleasant trip.
notes.practice: Repair: I wish you have a good weekend.
notes.answer: I hope you have a good weekend / Have a good weekend!

notes.title: Cleaner, not more cleaner
notes.explanation: Many short adjectives use -er. Longer adjectives often use more. Avoid combining both markers for the same ordinary comparison.
notes.qualification: Compare equivalent things: a price with a price, not a price with a shop.
notes.practice: Repair: This route is more shorter.
notes.answer: This route is shorter.

notes.title: Listen or hear?
notes.prompt:
I listened.
But did I hear?
notes.explanation: Listen to focuses on paying attention. Hear focuses on perceiving a sound. Remember to after listen when naming its object.
notes.qualification: Hearing is not always accidental: I can hear you is about perception.
examples: I could hear music next door.
notes.practice: Complete: Please listen ___ the recording.
notes.answer: to: Please listen to the recording.

notes.title: Remember or remind?
notes.explanation: Remember means have or bring something to mind. Remind means cause someone to remember or think about something.
notes.qualification: Use remind someone of something, or remind someone to do something.
examples: That song reminds me of summer.
The song brings a memory back.
notes.practice: Complete: Please ___ me to check my notes.
notes.answer: remind: Please remind me to check my notes.

notes.title: Remember doing or to do?
notes.explanation: Remember doing means recall an experience. Remember to do means not forget a task that needs doing.
notes.qualification: The verb form changes the meaning; neither pattern is automatically wrong.
notes.practice: You are giving a reminder before someone leaves. Choose: Remember locking / to lock the door.
notes.answer: Remember to lock the door.

notes.title: Memorise, remember, memory
notes.explanation: Memorise means deliberately learn something for later recall. Remember is broader. Memory is a noun for the ability or an experience recalled.
notes.qualification: Memorize is the usual American spelling; memorise is common in British English.
examples: I have fond memories of that trip.
notes.practice: Complete: This is one of my happiest ___. (memory)
notes.answer: memories: one of my happiest memories.

notes.title: Recognise or remember?
notes.prompt:
A familiar face.
A forgotten name.
notes.explanation: Recognise means identify something or someone as familiar. Remember means retain or recall information.
notes.qualification: You can recognise a person without remembering their name.
examples: I could not remember her name.
The name did not come to mind.
notes.practice: Complete: I ___ the melody, but I cannot remember the title.
notes.answer: recognise: I recognise the melody, but I cannot remember the title.

notes.title: See or meet?
notes.explanation: Meet can describe a planned meeting or an unexpected encounter. See can mean perceive visually or visit someone.
notes.qualification: Run into and bump into make an unexpected encounter especially clear.
examples: We met by chance at a café.
I am seeing a friend tomorrow.
notes.practice: Is We met by chance incorrect because meet must be planned?
notes.answer: No. Meet can describe both arranged and chance encounters.

notes.title: Approach or go up to?
notes.prompt:
approach the desk
go up to the desk
notes.explanation: Approach takes a direct object. Go up to includes to. Both can describe moving closer to a person or a thing.
notes.qualification: Approach is often more formal; choose the wording that suits the situation.
examples: I went up to the counter.
notes.practice: Repair: I approached to the window.
notes.answer: I approached the window / I went up to the window.

notes.title: Cook, cooker, or chef?
notes.prompt:
A great cook.
An electric cooker.
notes.explanation: A cook is a person who prepares food. A chef is a professional cook. A cooker is a cooking appliance, especially in British English.
notes.qualification: Cook is also a verb: I cook at home.
examples: My friend is a great cook.
notes.practice: Choose: The restaurant hired a new chef / cooker.
notes.answer: chef: a professional who prepares food.

notes.title: Staff or stuff?
notes.explanation: Staff refers to employees collectively. Stuff is an informal uncountable word for things or material.
notes.qualification: Use a member of staff or a staff member for one employee. Staff agreement varies by dialect and context.
examples: A member of staff helped me.
I left my stuff in a locker.
notes.practice: Complete: Could a member of ___ help me?
notes.answer: staff: Could a member of staff help me?

notes.title: Embarrassed or embarrassing?
notes.prompt:
I felt embarrassed.
It was embarrassing.
notes.explanation: Embarrassed describes the feeling. Embarrassing describes what causes it. Embarrassment is the noun.
notes.qualification: After feel, an adjective is often natural. After cause, a noun can fit.
examples: I felt embarrassed about the mix-up.
notes.practice: Repair: The mistake made me embarrassment.
notes.answer: The mistake made me embarrassed / The mistake caused embarrassment.

notes.title: Proud or arrogant?
notes.prompt:
proud of your work
arrogant towards others
notes.explanation: Proud can express satisfaction in an achievement. Arrogant describes behaving as if you are superior to other people.
notes.qualification: Pride has several meanings; context determines whether it is positive or negative.
examples: She takes pride in her work.
His arrogant tone upset the team.
notes.practice: Complete: I am proud ___ the progress I have made.
notes.answer: of: I am proud of the progress I have made.

notes.title: Competition or rivalry?
notes.explanation: Competition can name an organised event. Rivalry describes a competitive relationship, often over time. They are not interchangeable in every sentence.
notes.qualification: Contest often fits an event. It or the event can reduce repetition without changing the meaning.
examples: There is a rivalry between the teams.
notes.practice: Choose: She won the singing contest / rivalry.
notes.answer: contest: the sentence refers to an organised event.

notes.title: Award, prize, or reward?
notes.prompt:
win a prize
receive a reward
notes.explanation: An award recognises achievement. A prize is something won. A reward is a benefit or payment for an action or service.
notes.qualification: The meanings can overlap. Choose a word that matches why something was given.
examples: There is a reward for finding the bag.
notes.practice: Choose a natural word: Our team won first ___ in the contest.
notes.answer: prize: Our team won first prize in the contest.

notes.title: Many or various?
notes.explanation: Many emphasises quantity. Various emphasises different examples or kinds. Diverse highlights variety or differences.
notes.qualification: A number of means several or a quantity of; it does not always mean very many.
examples: The shop sells various types of notebook.
notes.practice: Which better highlights different kinds: many options or various options?
notes.answer: Various options highlights variety. Many options highlights quantity.

notes.title: What does multiple mean?
notes.explanation: Multiple means more than one. It does not tell us whether the items come from one shop or several shops.
notes.qualification: To express convenience, say I can get everything I need in one place.
examples: I got everything in one place.
notes.practice: Does I bought multiple items tell us how many shops I visited?
notes.answer: No. It tells us there was more than one item, not how many shops.

notes.title: Buy, purchase, or get?
notes.prompt:
I bought a book.
I got a book.
notes.explanation: Buy means obtain by paying. Purchase is usually more formal. Get has a broader meaning and does not always involve payment.
notes.qualification: Ordinary words such as buy are completely natural in spoken English.
examples: Payment is part of the meaning.
I got a book for my birthday.
It may have been a gift.
notes.practice: Does I got a book always mean I paid for it?
notes.answer: No. Get can mean receive, borrow, buy, or obtain in other ways; context decides.

notes.title: Rent or buy?
notes.prompt:
rent a bike
buy a bike
notes.explanation: Rent means pay to use something temporarily. Buy means pay to obtain ownership.
notes.qualification: Borrow usually means use something temporarily and return it, without paying a rental fee.
examples: We rented bikes for the afternoon.
notes.practice: You pay to use a boat for one hour. Did you rent it or buy it?
notes.answer: You rented it.

notes.title: Three ways to talk about rest
notes.prompt:
unwind
clear my head
take a break
notes.explanation: Unwind means relax after tension or effort. Clear my head means make thinking feel clearer. Take a break means pause an activity.
notes.qualification: These expressions overlap, but describe different aspects of resting.
examples: I read for a while to unwind.
A short walk helps me clear my head.
notes.practice: Complete: Let us take a ___ from studying.
notes.answer: break: Let us take a break from studying.

notes.title: Convenient or compatible?
notes.explanation: Convenient means practical or suitable for your needs. Compatible describes things or people that can work well together.
notes.qualification: For relationships, get on well or have a lot in common may express the meaning more clearly.
examples: Is this a convenient time to call?
The software is compatible with my laptop.
notes.practice: Complete: The station is nearby, so the location is ___.
notes.answer: convenient: the location is practical for travel.

notes.title: A poem or poetry?
notes.explanation: Poem is countable: one poem, two poems. Poetry is normally uncountable when naming the art form or a body of poems.
notes.qualification: Use a piece of poetry when you need a countable unit.
notes.practice: Repair: She wrote two poetries.
notes.answer: She wrote two poems.

notes.title: The T in often
notes.explanation: Both pronunciations of often, with and without /t/, are accepted. A silent-letter shortcut should not mark either one as wrong.
notes.qualification: Listen to a dictionary recording in your chosen reference accent and use a comfortable form.
notes.practice: True or false: The /t/ in often must always be silent.
notes.answer: False. Both forms are accepted.

notes.title: The sound at the end of -ing
notes.explanation: The usual dictionary ending of -ing is /ɪŋ/. For /ŋ/, the back of the tongue makes the closure. Do not add a separate hard /ɡ/.
notes.qualification: Informal -in’ with /ɪn/ is a real accent and style variant, not the rule for every -ing ending.
examples: Two /ŋ/ sounds in this reference form.
notes.practice: Which sound normally ends sing: /n/, /ŋ/, or /ŋɡ/?
notes.answer: /ŋ/. There is no extra /ɡ/ in the reference pronunciation.

notes.title: Singer is not like finger
notes.explanation: In common reference pronunciations, singer has /ŋ/ without a separate /ɡ/. Finger contains /ŋɡ/.
notes.qualification: Learn the pronunciation of the whole word; the letters ng do not guarantee one pattern in every accent or word.
notes.practice: In these reference forms, which word includes /ɡ/: singer or finger?
notes.answer: finger. Other accents may realise these words differently.

notes.title: The sound in watch
notes.explanation: The spelling tch commonly represents the affricate /tʃ/: a stop and release as one sound. Do not reduce watch to a final /ʃ/.
notes.qualification: Butcher also has /tʃ/; it is not an exception requiring a separate extra /t/.
notes.practice: Does match end with /ʃ/ or /tʃ/?
notes.answer: /tʃ/. Practise catch, match, watch slowly, then in a short sentence.

notes.title: Know and write
notes.explanation: In familiar words beginning kn-, the k is silent. In words beginning wr-, the w is silent.
notes.qualification: These are useful word-initial patterns, not rules for every k–n or w–r sequence across words.
notes.practice: Which initial letters are silent in knife and wrist?
notes.answer: K in knife; W in wrist.

notes.title: The hidden B
notes.explanation: B is silent in words such as climb, thumb, debt, and doubt. Learning these word groups helps you recognise the pattern.
notes.qualification: Do not mute every b beside m or t. Member and obtain retain /b/.
notes.practice: Does obtain lose its /b/ because b is next to t?
notes.answer: No. Obtain retains /b/; this is not a universal letter-pair rule.

notes.title: Sign, but signal
notes.explanation: G is silent in sign, design, and gnome. A related word may pronounce it: signal and signature include /ɡ/.
notes.qualification: The spelling gn does not always mean silent g; magnet also includes /ɡ/.
notes.practice: Which has a /ɡ/ in the reference pronunciation: sign or signal?
notes.answer: signal. Compare sign /saɪn/ with signal /ˈsɪɡnəl/.

notes.title: When L is silent
notes.explanation: L is silent in common words such as walk, talk, calm, half, could, and would. Learn the words alongside the patterns.
notes.qualification: Always and shoulder keep /l/. Almond has accepted pronunciations with and without /l/.
notes.practice: Must almond have a silent L in every accepted pronunciation?
notes.answer: No. Accepted pronunciations include forms with and without /l/.

notes.title: GU and QU need a closer look
notes.explanation: Guess and guitar begin with /ɡ/, without /w/. Quick and queen begin with /kw/. These spellings do not follow one universal silent-U rule.
notes.qualification: Letters work together to represent sounds; not every written letter has a separate sound.
notes.practice: Does queen begin with /k/ alone or /kw/?
notes.answer: /kw/: queen /kwiːn/.

notes.title: Three sounds for SC
notes.explanation: SC is not always pronounced the same way. Compare scene, school, and conscious before applying a silent-C shortcut.
notes.qualification: Pronunciation belongs to the whole word, not just a pair of letters.
notes.practice: Which sound is represented by sc in conscious: /s/, /sk/, or /ʃ/?
notes.answer: /ʃ/ in common reference pronunciations of conscious.

notes.title: Hour, what, and who
notes.explanation: Hour and honest have a silent h. What and where usually begin with /w/. Who begins with /h/, without /w/.
notes.qualification: Some accents distinguish wh from w, so what can have a different initial sound.
examples: The next sound is a vowel.
notes.practice: Choose the article: a / an honest mistake.
notes.answer: an honest mistake, because honest begins with a vowel sound.

notes.title: Silent P, word by word
notes.explanation: P is silent in common pronunciations of psychology, pneumonia, cupboard, and raspberry. Recognise these words as useful groups.
notes.qualification: Upbeat keeps /p/: there is no universal rule that p disappears before b.
notes.practice: Does psychology begin with /p/, /ps/, or /s/?
notes.answer: /s/ in common reference pronunciations.

notes.title: Can or can’t?
notes.explanation: Use sentence meaning, stress, vowel quality, and consonant cues together. A clearly released /t/ is not the only clue to can’t.
notes.qualification: Can often has a weak form /kən/. The vowel in can’t differs across accents.
examples: Can may be unstressed and reduced.
Did you say you can or you can’t?
notes.practice: If you cannot hear a clear final /t/, must the word be can?
notes.answer: No. The /t/ may lack an audible release or have another realisation. Check other cues or ask.

notes.title: Linking is not deletion
notes.prompt:
A quiet consonant
may still be there.
notes.explanation: Linking connects sounds across word boundaries. Elision omits a sound. An unreleased stop keeps its closure without a clear release burst.
notes.qualification: Do not delete every final /t/ or /d/ before another consonant.
examples: Some speakers may omit /t/ in this cluster.
notes.practice: If a stop has no audible release, does that prove it was deleted?
notes.answer: No. The articulatory closure may remain even without a distinct release burst.

notes.title: Three sounds for plural S
notes.explanation: Use /s/ after voiceless non-sibilants, /z/ after voiced non-sibilants, and /ɪz/ after sibilants such as /s, z, ʃ, ʒ, tʃ, dʒ/.
notes.qualification: Choose by the preceding sound, not the letter. Some accents use a different vowel in the extra syllable.
notes.practice: Which plural ending does bags take: /s/, /z/, or /ɪz/?
notes.answer: /z/, because /ɡ/ is a voiced non-sibilant.

notes.title: Various and diversity
notes.explanation: Various has first-syllable stress. Diversity has second-syllable stress. Practise the stressed syllable clearly, without giving every syllable equal weight.
notes.qualification: The capitals show stress only; use normal spelling in ordinary writing.
examples: Stress the first syllable of various.
Stress the second syllable of diversity.
notes.practice: Which syllable is stressed in diversity: first, second, or third?
notes.answer: The second syllable. Listen to a dictionary model and repeat it in a phrase.

notes.title: Same spelling, different vowels
notes.explanation: The spelling oo represents different vowels in these words. Learn a spelling pattern with examples and counterexamples.
notes.qualification: These are common reference forms. Accent differences can affect the vowels you hear.
examples: A third vowel in this reference accent
notes.practice: Does book have the same vowel as moon in these reference forms?
notes.answer: No. Book uses /ʊ/ and moon uses /uː/.

notes.title: Same sound, different word
notes.explanation: Homophones share a pronunciation in a particular accent, but their meanings or spellings differ. Context helps you identify the word.
notes.qualification: Not every pair matches in every accent: aunt and ant may sound the same or different.
examples: I will buy it by Friday.
buy = purchase; by = no later than
notes.practice: Complete: I can ___ the sea. (see / sea)
notes.answer: see: I can see the sea.

notes.title: Sounds can adapt
notes.explanation: In connected speech, a sound may adapt to a neighbour. In ten bucks, /n/ may become [m]. In did you, /d/ + /j/ may combine as [dʒ].
notes.qualification: These are possible realisations, not compulsory changes or spelling rules.
notes.practice: If /n/ becomes [m] before /b/, is that assimilation or deletion?
notes.answer: Assimilation: the sound changes rather than simply disappearing.

notes.title: Accent is not a ranking
notes.prompt:
car · water
Same words.
Different accents.
notes.explanation: Many American accents pronounce the r in car. Some British accents do not in isolation. American water often contains a flap [ɾ].
notes.qualification: British and American accents both vary. A flap is not simply the ordinary English r sound.
examples: A brief tongue-tip contact in many US accents
notes.practice: Are mixed accent features automatically pronunciation errors?
notes.answer: No. Aim for intelligibility and learn to recognise accent variation.

notes.title: Describe more than an adjective
notes.prompt:
It is nice.
What makes it nice?
notes.explanation: Build a description from one clear detail and its effect on you: place → detail → personal meaning.
notes.qualification: Choose useful details instead of listing adjectives. This is a flexible practice framework, not a required exam formula.
examples: The reading room has large windows, so it feels bright even on cloudy days.
A visible detail explains the impression.
What I like most is the quiet / the natural light / the comfortable seating.
Choose one feature and explain why it matters.
notes.practice: Describe a fictional study space in two sentences. Include a detail and its effect.
notes.answer: One possible answer: The room has a desk beside the window. The natural light makes it a pleasant place to read.

notes.title: Give your story a turning point
notes.explanation: Use setting → unexpected change → response → outcome. Keep the main events in a clear time order.
notes.qualification: Use past perfect when it helps show an earlier event; do not add it to every past sentence.
examples: I was waiting for the bus when I realised I had left my bag at home.
I went back for it and caught the next bus. In the end, I arrived on time.
notes.practice: Continue this fictional story: I was about to give a presentation when the screen went blank…
notes.answer: One possible answer: I explained the main idea without the slides. A colleague fixed the screen, and I continued with the examples.

notes.title: Develop an opinion
notes.explanation: Try position → reason → example → qualification. Explain why your example supports your view.
notes.qualification: A qualification can show the limits of your claim. You do not need to force four steps into every short answer.
examples: I think libraries still matter because they give people access to books without buying them.
For example, students can borrow textbooks. However, opening hours affect how useful the service is.
notes.practice: Give one reason for keeping public libraries, then add one limitation.
notes.answer: One possible answer: Libraries offer quiet study space, but they need suitable opening hours to serve more people.

notes.title: Describe what you can see
notes.prompt:
I can see…
They might be…
notes.explanation: State visible details directly. Use might, seems, or appears when you infer something the picture does not establish.
notes.qualification: A picture alone rarely proves someone’s occupation, relationship, diagnosis, or emotion.
examples: Two people are sitting at a table with notebooks.
They might be preparing for a meeting.
A possible interpretation, not a fact
notes.practice: A picture shows someone holding a suitcase. Write one observation and one cautious inference.
notes.answer: One possible answer: The person is holding a suitcase. They might be about to travel.

notes.title: Make convenient specific
notes.explanation: Name the practical benefit: less travel, fewer steps, more choice, or easier access. Then give one concrete detail.
notes.qualification: A precise everyday explanation is often stronger than a formal synonym.
examples: The shop is convenient because I can buy groceries and household items in one place.
The site saves me time / is easy to navigate / lets me compare prices.
Choose the benefit that actually fits.
notes.practice: Replace This app is convenient with a sentence explaining a practical benefit.
notes.answer: One possible answer: This app lets me check train times without visiting several websites.

notes.title: Polite restaurant English
notes.prompt:
I would like…
Could I have…?
notes.explanation: Use I would like to state an order. Use Could I have…? for a polite request. Would you like…? offers something to another person.
notes.qualification: I want is grammatical, but can sound blunt when ordering. Tone and context matter too.
examples: I would like the vegetable soup, please.
Could we have the bill / a glass of water / the menu, please?
notes.practice: You are offering a drink. Choose: I would like / Would you like some water?
notes.answer: Would you like some water? This is an offer, not your own request.

notes.title: Explain a problem clearly
notes.prompt:
What went wrong?
What help do you need?
notes.explanation: Use problem → what you tried → request. Give enough detail for the other person to act.
notes.qualification: Access is a verb with a direct object: access the file. As a noun, it can take to: access to the file.
examples: I cannot open the file. I have tried downloading it again, but that has not helped.
Could you send another copy / check the link / help me open it?
Ask for a specific next step.
notes.practice: Write a two-sentence request about a broken link.
notes.answer: One possible answer: The link does not open, even in another browser. Could you check it and send a new one?

notes.title: Ask instead of guessing
notes.prompt:
Could you repeat that?
Do you mean…?
notes.explanation: Ask for repetition when you missed the words. Ask for clarification when you heard the words but are unsure of the meaning.
notes.qualification: Confirm important details directly instead of pretending you understood.
examples: Could you say that again a little more slowly?
By draft, do you mean the first version?
notes.practice: You are unsure whether the speaker said can or cannot. What could you ask?
notes.answer: Did you say you can or you cannot? / Just to check, are you able to do it?

notes.title: Pause, repair, continue
notes.prompt:
Let me think.
What I mean is…
notes.explanation: A short pause can help you organise an answer. If you notice a meaningful error, correct the phrase briefly and continue.
notes.qualification: Do not restart a whole answer for every small slip. Repeated fillers can also interrupt the listener.
examples: Let me think for a moment. The main reason is…
We go there yesterday—sorry, we went there yesterday.
notes.practice: Repair only the tense: Last weekend, I buy a new notebook.
notes.answer: Last weekend, I bought a new notebook. You can correct buy to bought without restarting the whole story.

notes.title: Because or because of?
notes.prompt:
because it rained
because of the rain
notes.explanation: Because introduces a clause with a subject and verb. Because of is followed by a noun phrase or an -ing phrase.
notes.qualification: Choose the structure that fits the next words, not whichever sounds more advanced.
examples: We stayed inside because it was raining.
We stayed inside because of the rain.
notes.practice: Complete: The match was delayed ___ bad weather.
notes.answer: because of: The match was delayed because of bad weather.

notes.title: But, although, however
notes.prompt:
It was late, but…
Although it was late…
notes.explanation: But joins contrasting clauses. Although introduces a subordinate clause. However links ideas and normally needs a sentence boundary or semicolon in writing.
notes.qualification: In the standard pattern, do not pair Although… with but to join the same two clauses.
examples: Although it was late, we kept talking.
It was late. However, we kept talking.
notes.practice: Repair: Although the café was busy, but we found a seat.
notes.answer: Although the café was busy, we found a seat / The café was busy, but we found a seat.

notes.title: If or in case?
notes.prompt:
if it rains
in case it rains
notes.explanation: If introduces a condition. In case often introduces a reason for taking a precaution before a possible event.
notes.qualification: In these future-time examples, use present simple after if or in case, rather than automatically adding will.
examples: Take an umbrella in case it rains.
Take it now as a precaution.
If it rains, we will stay inside.
Rain is the condition for the plan.
notes.practice: You save a backup now because your laptop might fail. Choose: if / in case it fails.
notes.answer: in case it fails: Save a backup in case your laptop fails.

notes.title: Examples or exact details?
notes.explanation: For example introduces an illustration. Such as introduces examples within a phrase. Namely specifies exactly what or who you mean.
notes.qualification: Do not use namely when you are only giving a few examples from a larger group.
examples: I enjoy outdoor activities such as walking and cycling.
We need two items, namely a pen and a notebook.
notes.practice: Complete: There is one problem, ___ the cost.
notes.answer: namely: you are specifying the exact problem.

notes.title: Eventually or overall?
notes.prompt:
Eventually, we arrived.
Overall, it went well.
notes.explanation: Eventually means something happens after time, difficulty, or delay. Overall introduces a general judgement after considering the whole situation.
notes.qualification: Finally can mark a final point in a list or an eventual result; context decides.
examples: After two delays, we eventually reached the station.
notes.practice: Choose: Eventually / Overall, the course was useful, despite a few difficult lessons.
notes.answer: Overall: the sentence gives an evaluation of the course as a whole.

notes.title: Compare on a clear basis
notes.prompt:
Better for what?
Better for whom?
notes.explanation: Choose one comparison point at a time: portability, focus, cost, or search. Explain the trade-off instead of claiming one option wins for everyone.
notes.qualification: Compare equivalent things, and separate your preference from a universal claim.
examples: E-books are easier to carry, while paper books let me read without screen notifications.
I prefer paper for long reading sessions, but digital books are useful when I travel.
notes.practice: Compare online and in-person shopping using one benefit of each.
notes.answer: One possible answer: Online shopping saves travel time, while in-person shopping lets me check the fit before buying.

notes.title: Make a claim you can support
notes.prompt:
Everyone does it?
Or some people?
notes.explanation: Match the strength of your claim to the evidence. Some, often, may, and in my experience can keep a statement accurate.
notes.qualification: Do not add an exact statistic unless you have checked its source and date. Specific examples can be enough.
examples: Some shops have closed as more customers buy online.
A limited claim about a business trend
Technology can change shopping habits, though the effect varies by business.
notes.practice: Make this claim more careful: All children hate reading.
notes.answer: One possible answer: Some children are reluctant to read, and their interest may depend on the books available.
